courses.description: Human thought and meaning are deeply tied to the capacity for mapping conceptual domains onto each other, inducing common schemas and performing mental simulation. This course examines major aspects of this cognitive activity including metaphor, conceptual blending, and embodied cognition.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Upper-Division Seminar on Special Topics
courses.description: Special topics in cognitive science are discussed. (May be repeated when topics vary.)
courses.prerequisites_text: department approval.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Neuroimaging of Cognition
courses.description: Introduction to functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) methods for cognitive neuroscience research. This course will cover basic aspects of the physics and biological principles underlying MRI and fMRI, technical aspects of experimental design and data collection for fMRI, as well as basic data processing and analysis approaches.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 107B or COGS 107C or PSYC 106 or PSYC 108.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Space and Time in the Brain
courses.description: The course examines features of neural dynamics that map spatial and temporal relationships. Lectures will cover interval timing, mapping of item-to-observer position, mapping of observer-to-world position, and the conjunction of spatial and temporal coding in hippocampus.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Usability and Information Architecture
courses.description: Examines the cognitive basis of successful web and multimedia design. Topics: information architecture, navigation, usability, graphic layout, transaction design, and how to understand user interaction.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 18 or CSE 11 or CSE 8A and COGS 10 or DSGN 1.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Brain Computer Interfaces
courses.description: This course will discuss signal processing, pattern recognition algorithms, and human-computer interaction issues in EEG-based brain-computer interfaces. Other types of brain-computer interfaces will also be discussed.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 108 or COGS 109 or COGS 118A or COGS 118B.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Pre-Honors Project in Cognitive Science
courses.description: This course prepares students for the Cognitive Science Honors Program. The aim is to refine the research project and to teach students what a successfully written proposal entails. Students may be admitted to the Honors Program contingent upon completion and progress in the course. See “ Cognitive Science Honors Program ” section for more information. Course should be taken for a letter grade.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing; instructor and department approval.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Pedagogy and Learning Apprenticeship
courses.description: Under the supervision of an instructor, undergraduate students gain teaching experience through practical experiences in course management and effective teaching methods. P/NP grades only. May be taken for credit two times.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing; 3.0 GPA; instructor and department approval.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Cognitive Science Internship
courses.description: The student will undertake a program of practical research in a supervised work environment. Topics to be researched may vary, but in each case the course will provide skills for carrying out these studies. P/NP grades only. May be taken for credit up to three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing; 2.5 GPA; department approval.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Special Project
courses.description: This independent study course is for individual, advanced students who wish to complete a one-quarter reading or research project under the mentorship of a faculty member. Students should contact faculty whose research interests them to discuss possible projects. P/NP grades only. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing; 2.5 GPA; consent of instructor and department approval.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Cognitive Science Foundations: Theories and Methods in the Study of Cognitive Phenomena
courses.description: Surveys a variety of theoretical and methodological approaches to the study of human cognition. Topics include language structure, language processing, concepts and categories, knowledge representation, analogy and metaphor, reasoning, planning and action, problem solving, learning and expertise, and emotion.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Introduction to Research
courses.description: This sequence is an intensive research project. Students under faculty mentorship perform a thorough analysis of the problem and the literature, carry out original studies, and prepare oral and written presentations. Students should aim for a report of publishable quality. Letter grade required.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Research Methods in Cognitive Science
courses.description: Issues in design, implementation, and evaluation of research in cognitive science are discussed. Students will present and comment on their own research projects in progress. Discussions also include presentations of research to various audiences, abstracts, reviews, grant process, and scientific ethics. Letter grade required.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Design at Large
courses.description: (Cross-listed with DSGN 219 and CSE 219.) New societal challenges, cultural values, and technological opportunities are changing design, and vice versa. The seminar explores this increased scale, real-world engagement, and disruptive impact. Invited speakers from UC San Diego and beyond share cutting-edge research on interaction, design, and learning. S/U grades only. May be taken for credit up to eighteen times. Students may receive a combined total of eighteen units for COGS 229, CSE 219, and DSGN 219.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Topics in Human-Computer Interaction
courses.description: (Cross-listed with CSE 216.) Prepares students to conduct original HCI research by reading and discussing seminal and cutting-edge research papers. Topics include design, social software, input techniques, mobile, and ubiquitous computing. Student pairs perform a quarter-long mini research project that leverages campus research efforts. Letter grades only.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Foundations for Future User Interfaces
courses.description: This course will cover the fundamental elements of effective human-computer interaction (HCI), including input modalities and techniques, representations, etc. In this course, the student will take a deep dive into classic literature in HCI, and in doing so identify fundamental problems that remain in today’s user interfaces as well as proposing and developing exciting alternative user interface concepts.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Seminar on Special Topics
courses.description: Specific topics in cognitive science are discussed. (May be repeated when topics vary.)

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Cognitive Science Laboratory Rotation
courses.description: Laboratory rotations provide students with experience in the various experimental methods used in cognitive science.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor. S/U only.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Directed Independent Study
courses.description: Students study and research selected topics under the direction of a member of the faculty.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Introduction to Communication
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the history, theory, and practice of communication. Topics covered include language literacy, representation, semiotics, mediated technologies, institutional formations, and social interaction. Course work may involve media production (for example, writing, video and media production, or performance). No credit for COMM 10 if taken after COMM 10R.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Analysis of Audio/Visual Media: Form, Style, and Meaning
courses.description: This course builds the critical skills to understand, analyze, interpret audio/visual media by introducing students to the basic vocabulary and grammar of audio and moving image texts—how they create meaning through compositional form and narrative style—and key critical methodologies for interpreting media culture. Concepts covered will lay the groundwork for continued study in scholarly communication areas and hands-on sound, film/video, and/or social media production. No credit for COMM 20 if taken after COMM 20R.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Introduction to Promotional Communication
courses.description: A critical-cultural communication introduction to fields of practice that publicize, promote, or increase awareness of brands, ideas, products, and causes. Exploration of public communication industries and practices, the pressures that shape these industries and practices, and their implications for culture and society. Course will address major promotional industries such as advertising, public relations, marketing, and social media.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Presenting and Public Speaking
courses.description: This course covers the basics of communication in public and professional settings. Students will cultivate their own speaking style while developing skills in delivery, performance, and persuasion. They will learn how to create a slide deck as well as prepare for speeches, interviews, and Q and As.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Public Presentation and Persuasion—Speech and Debate
courses.description: Throughout history, important advances in a democratic society have emerged most often from civil, rigorous discussion, debate, and persuasion. Students develop research, critical thinking, presentation, public speaking, and argumentation skills through in-class practice speeches and debates, along with participation in intercollegiate speech and debate tournaments. May be taken for credit up to six times.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Communication, the Person, and Everyday Life
courses.description: This course is a critical introduction to processes of interaction within lived and built environments. It includes historical survey of theories and methods including actor network-theory, conversation analysis, ethnography, ethnomethodology, cultural linguistics, performance, and social cognition. Course work may integrate scholarly study with production (e.g., in-context observation and research or audio/video production).
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Introduction to Audiovisual Media Practices
courses.description: This upper-division course is required as the gateway to all future communication media production courses. Students will learn about contemporary media practices such as film, video, digital/online, and social media production, and how these practices are formed by technical and social constraints. In the studio portion of this course, students will work hands-on with video and new media equipment to apply what they have learned.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: MPL: Documentary Sketchbook
courses.description: Digital video is the medium used in this class both as a production technology and as a device to explore the theory and practice of documentary production. Technical demonstrations, lectures, production exercises, and readings will emphasize the interrelation between production values and ethics, problems of representation, and documentary history. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and COMM 101.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: MPL: Communication and Computers
courses.description: This course introduces students to computers as media of communication. Each quarter, students participate in a variety of networking activities designed to show the interactive potential of the medium. Fieldwork designed to teach basic methods is combined with readings designed to build a deeper theoretical understanding of computer-based communication.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: MPL: Sound Production and Manipulation
courses.description: This hands-on course serves as an introduction to sound production, design, and editing. Students create projects by recording original sounds and editing on a digital audio workstation. We consider the potential of sound in film, radio, TV, and on the web by reviewing work and reading sound theory. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 101 or VIS 70N.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: MPL: Topics in Production
courses.description: Specialized study in production with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter. Students will use audio/film studios, editing rooms, and cameras to produce media work in a variety of forms for various presentation platforms that can include documentary shorts, radio plays, or digital images. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 101 or COGN 22 or VIS 70N prerequisites can be taken concurrently by permission.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: MMPP: Practicum in New Media and Community Life
courses.description: A combined lecture/lab in a specially designed after-school setting in southeastern San Diego working with children and adults. Students design new media and produce special projects, and explore issues related to human development, social justice, and community life. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: none

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Introduction to Media Industries
courses.description: Introduction to topics that arise across various media industries, including media economics, ownership and consolidation in media, media regulation and deregulation, media technologies, creative labor, intellectual property, financialization, globalization, and ethics in media. Engage directly with current events, read recent coverage in the trade press, and learn to analyze contemporary media companies and systems.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: CI: Film Industry
courses.description: A study of the social organization of the film industry throughout its history. Who makes films, by what criteria, and for what audience? The changing relationships between studios, producers, directors, writers, actors, editors, censors, distributors, audience, and subject matter of the films will be explored.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Journalism and the News Industry
courses.description: Survey the development of journalism as a profession and news media as an industry and social institution. How to understand the production of news, the forces that shape social representations in the news, access to the public sphere, and approaches to the analysis of news media content. Debates about ethical issues in journalism, “objectivity” and the politics of news, and the sustainability of journalism as an institution. No credit for COMM 106N if taken after COMM 106NR.
courses.prerequisites_text: junior or senior standing.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: POB: Disability
courses.description: Cultural and historical ways of defining and understanding disability relative to communication and assistive technologies, including the impact of digital technologies and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Course use of audiovisual texts and writings from fields including science and technology studies, and cultural studies.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Intermediate Topics in Communication
courses.description: Specialized study of communication topics, to be determined by the instructor, for any given quarter. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: CSI: Gender, Labor, and Culture in the Global Economy
courses.description: This course introduces students to different theories of globalization and of gender. Against this theoretical background, students critically examine the gendered (and racialized) nature of labor in the production of material, social, and cultural goods in the global economy.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: CSI: Media Technologies and Social Movements
courses.description: Course explores the roles of media technologies in activist campaigns, social movements. Blending theory, historical case studies, and project-based group work, students will investigate possibilities and limitations of attempts to enroll new and old media technologies in collective efforts to make social change.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Communication and the Senses
courses.description: While we often assume that communication is something that happens only with our eyes and/or ears, every act of communication is multisensory, often involving sight and sound but also smell, touch, and taste. In this course, students will learn how to pay attention to and engage with the “other” senses beyond the visual and auditory. Interdisciplinary scholarship and empirical activities help students build a vocabulary for understanding the complexities of multisensory communication.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Advanced Persuasion
courses.description: This course instructs advanced strategies, tactics, and presentation skills necessary for superior performance in intercollegiate speech and debate competitions. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 80.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: AMP: Media Stereotypes
courses.description: An examination of how the media present society’s members and activities in stereotypical formats. Reasons for and consequences of this presentation are examined. Student responsibilities will be (a) participation in measurement and analysis of stereotype presentations. (b) investigating techniques for assessing both cognitive and behavioral effects of such scripted presentations on the users of media. Students will not receive credit for COMT 105 and COMM 120M.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and two of COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Problem of Voice
courses.description: This course will explore the problem of self-expression for members of various ethnic and cultural groups. Of special interest is how writers find ways of describing themselves in the face of others’ sometimes overwhelming predilection to describe them.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Television and Citizenship
courses.description: Television is a contested site for negotiating the rationales of inclusion and exclusion associated with citizenship and national belonging. Historical and contemporary case studies within international comparative contexts consider regulation, civil rights, cultural difference, social movements, new technologies, and globalization.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Media Audiences
courses.description: Examines the complex relationship between mass media and the consumers and viewers they target. This course covers theories about audiences, reading practices of audiences, the economics of audiences, and the role of audiences in the digital era.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Contemporary Minority Media Makers and the Festival Experience
courses.description: This advanced course examines, analyzes, and discusses media works by contemporary Asian American, Native American, African American, and Latina/o American filmmakers. The course does not offer a historical survey of films by minority makers but rather will operate on themes such as cultural identity, urbanization, personal relationships, gender relations, cultural retentions, and music. The course will require students to attend some off-campus screenings, especially those at area film festivals.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Film Authorship
courses.description: This course examines film authorship by focusing on two filmmakers and exploring the many ways that films are authored and produce meaning. Students learn how to analyze a film’s production, collaboration, representation, reception, and industrial context, in order to explore broader themes and social issues such as race, class, gender, violence, and authorial responsibility. Film authors may include Spike Lee, Kathryn Bigelow, Bong Joon-ho, or Alfonso Cuarón.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Advanced Topics in Cultural Production
courses.description: Specialized advanced study in cultural production with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Global Cultures of K-Pop
courses.description: Examine the sprawling, often contradictory cultural terrain of K-pop, South Korea’s multi-billion-dollar pop music industry. Consider the broad range of social and technological structures, creative practices, emotional attachments, and embedded value systems that have been cultivated by the industry across a range of geopolitical contexts. Explore different sets of issues and case studies anchored in critical concepts drawn from assigned readings, lectures, and experiential exercises.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40, or COMM 50.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Behind the Internet: Invisible Geographies of Power and Inequality
courses.description: This course aims to unveil the vast and largely hidden infrastructures silently shaping how digital communication take place in contemporary societies as well as the visible and invisible geographic of power and inequality these infrastructures are helping to create.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Interaction with Technology
courses.description: In this class we will look closely at the everyday ways in which we interact with technology to discuss sociocultural character of objects, built environments; situated, distributed, and embodied character of knowledges; use of multimodal semiotic resources, talk, gesture, body orientation, and gaze in interaction with technology.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Culture, Domination, and Resistance
courses.description: Explores theories and narratives of cultural power, contemporary practices of resistance. Texts from a wide range of disciplines consider how domination is enacted, enforced, and what modes of resistance are employed to contend with uses and abuses of political power.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Communication for Indigenous Justice
courses.description: The course provides students the opportunity to learn from indigenous scholarship, activism, and art. It introduces students to indigenous justice issues such as knowledge production, environmental stewardship, cultural appropriation, and stereotyped representations—all within the contexts of settler colonialism and indigenous resistance and survival. It gives students tools to examine those issues from communication and media studies perspectives and to explore ways to promote indigenous justice.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Junior Seminar in Communication
courses.description: The junior seminar enables a detailed examination of a specific topic from the field of communication selected by the instructor, exploring in greater depth theories and methods introduced in the core communication curriculum. Seminars are limited to thirty students with a heavy focus on class participation. Students complete a research project with a significant final product (typically a research paper). No credit for COMM 190 if taken after COMM 190R.
courses.prerequisites_text: junior or senior standing and COMM 10 and at least one from COMM 100A-B-C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Research Seminar in Washington, D.C.
courses.description: (Same as POLI 194, USP 194, HITO 193, SOCI 194, and COGS 194) Course attached to six-unit internship taken by students participating in the UCDC program. Involves weekly seminar meetings with faculty and teaching assistants and a substantial research paper.
courses.prerequisites_text: participation in UCDC program.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Honors Seminar in Communication I: Methods
courses.description: Preparation of an honors thesis, which can be either a research paper or a media production project. Open to students who have been admitted to the honors program. Grades will be awarded upon completion of the two-quarter sequence.
courses.prerequisites_text: admission to the departmental honors program.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Independent Study in Communication
courses.description: Independent study and research under the direction of a member of the faculty. May be taken three times for credit.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor. (P/NP grades only.)

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Introduction to the Study of Communication as Social Force
courses.description: This course focuses on descriptive and analytical approaches to the political economy of communication and social organization of media institutions. Texts will emphasize the complex structure of communication industries (historically and cross-nationally) and will examine causal and theoretical relationships between social structures, media institutions, public opinion, consumption, and voting. Restricted to major code CM75.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Introduction to the Study of Communication: Communication and the Individual
courses.description: This course will draw on theorists who examine human nature as constituted by social, material, and historical circumstances. This course considers the media in relation to the ontogenetic and historical development of the human being and an examination of the individual as socially constituted in a language-using medium. The role of new communication technologies as part of research methodologies is explored in lecture-seminar. Restricted to major code CM75.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Introduction to Science Studies: Part 1
courses.description: Study and discussion of classic themes and texts in history of science, sociology of science, and philosophy of science, and of work that attempts to develop an interdisciplinary science studies approach.
courses.prerequisites_text: enrollment in the Science Studies Program or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Colloquium in Science Studies
courses.description: A forum for the presentation and discussion of research in progress in science studies by graduate students, faculty, and visitors. Students must attend the colloquium series for their entire first and second years. They receive course credit in one quarter each year.
courses.prerequisites_text: enrollment in the Science Studies Program.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Topics in Communication
courses.description: Specialized study in communication, with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Graduate Research
courses.description: Advanced independent study in communication under the guidance of Department of Communication faculty.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Practice Teaching in Communication
courses.description: A doctoral student in communication is required to assist in teaching undergraduate Department of Communication courses for a total of six quarters. One meeting per week with the instructor, one meeting per week with the assigned sections, and attendance at the lecture of the undergraduate course in which he or she is participating are part of this requirement.

courses.subject: CSS
courses.title: Introductory Programming for Computational Social Science
courses.description: This course develops computational thinking practices and skills critical for defining, describing, and analyzing social science problems using a computational approach. Students will learn to program in Python in the context of computational social science problems.

courses.subject: CSS
courses.title: Environmental Data Science
courses.description: This is an upper-division course focused on understanding some of the many approaches, algorithms, and processes used in environmental sciences. We will consider topics such as predicting fires using satellite data, analyzing strategies to improve conservation, and understanding the use of time series data for environmental purposes. Students will be taught to make predictions of migration patterns, temperatures, rising ocean levels, limitations in water sources, and crop growths.

courses.subject: CSS
courses.title: Computational Social Science Research Seminar
courses.description: A weekly seminar series focused on selected topics in computational social science.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing.

courses.subject: CSS
courses.title: Research in Computational Social Science
courses.description: Independent research under the supervision of individual faculty members.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing.

courses.subject: CSS
courses.title: Teaching Apprentice
courses.description: Graduate students are required to enroll in a teaching assistantship course while supporting undergraduate courses.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Fluency in Information Technology
courses.description: Introduces the concepts and skills necessary to effectively use information technology. Includes basic concepts and some practical skills with computer and networks.
courses.prerequisites_text: none.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Science and Object-Oriented Programming: Python
courses.description: An introduction to computer science and programming using the Python language. The course will cover topics such as basic data types (e.g., integer, float, string), loops and iteration, basic data structures (e.g., list, set, dictionary), memory models, conditional statements, recursion, basic algorithm time complexity analysis, class design, and inheritance. A student may not receive credit for CSE 6R after receiving credit for CSE 8A, CSE 8B, CSE 11, or COGS 18. Students may receive credit for only one of the following: COGS 18, CSE 8A, or CSE 6R. Recommended preparation: a familiarity with high school-level algebra is expected, but this course assumes no prior programming knowledge or experience.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Programming and Computational Problem-Solving I
courses.description: Introductory course for students interested in computer science and programming. Basics of programming including variables, conditionals, loops, functions/methods. Structured data storage such as arrays/lists and dictionaries, including data mutation. Hands-on experience with designing, writing, hand-tracing, compiling or interpreting, executing, testing, and debugging programs. Students solve relevant computational problems using a high-level programming language. CSE 8A is part of a two-course sequence (CSE 8A-B) that is equivalent to CSE 11. Students should take CSE 8B to complete the CSE 8A/CSE 8B track. Students who have taken CSE 8B or CSE 11 may not take or receive credit for CSE 8A. Students may receive credit for one of the following: COGS 18, CSE 8A, or CSE 6R. Recommended preparation: No prior programming experience is assumed, but comfort using computers is helpful. Students should consult the “CSE Course Placement Advice” web page for assistance in choosing which CSE course to take first.
courses.prerequisites_text: restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Programming and Computational Problem-Solving: Accelerated Pace
courses.description: Accelerated introductory programming including an object-oriented approach. Covers basic programming topics from CSE 8A including variables, conditionals, loops, functions/methods, structured data storage, and mutation. Also covers topics from CSE 8B including the Java programming language, class design, interfaces, basic class hierarchies, recursion, event-based programming, and file I/O. Basics of command-line navigation for file management and running programs. Zero units of credit offered for CSE 11 if CSE 8B taken previously or concurrently. Recommended preparation: Significant prior programming experience (for example, high school AP CSA). Students should consult the “CSE Course Placement Advice” web page for assistance in choosing a first CSE course.
courses.prerequisites_text: restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Basic Data Structures and Object-Oriented Design
courses.description: Use and implementation of basic data structures including linked lists, stacks, and queues. Use of advanced structures such as binary trees and hash tables. Object-oriented design including interfaces, polymorphism, encapsulation, abstract data types, pre-/post-conditions. Recursion. Uses Java and Java Collections.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 8B or CSE 11; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Discrete Mathematics
courses.description: This course will introduce the ways logic is used in computer science: for reasoning, as a language for specifications, and as operations in computation. Concepts include sets, relations, functions, equivalence relations, partial orders, number systems, and proof methods (especially induction and recursion). Propositional and predicate logic will be introduced and applied to various computer science domains such as circuit design, databases, cryptography, and program correctness. Students who have completed MATH 109 may not receive credit for CSE 20. Credit not offered for both MATH 15A and CSE 20. Equivalent to MATH 15A.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 11 or CSE 6R or CSE 8A or CSE 8B or ECE 15. Prerequisite courses must have been completed with a grade of C– or better; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Mathematics for Algorithms and Systems
courses.description: This course will cover mathematical concepts used to model and analyze algorithms and computer systems. Topics include counting techniques (inclusion-exclusion; recursive counting; permutations and combinations), data representations, analysis of algorithms (order notation; time complexities; loop invariants), recurrence relations, graphs and trees (data structure representations; basic graph algorithms; special classes of graphs), and basic probability and its applications.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 20 or MATH 15A or MATH 31CH; students who have completed MATH 154 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 previously or concurrently may not receive credit for CSE 21; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Systems Programming and Software Tools
courses.description: A programmer’s view of how computer systems execute programs, store information, and communicate. Emphasis on understanding the details of how a single computer program executes on a computer. Hands-on systems programming using the C programming language and software tools (e.g., gdb, valgrind, make) in the UNIX environment. Builds foundation for courses on computer organization, operating systems, networks, and compilers.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 11 or CSE 8B or ECE 15; two units of credit offered for CSE 29 if CSE 15L taken previously.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Computer Organization
courses.description: Introduction to organization of modern digital computers. Students learn how to write programs in assembly, design basic processors capable of executing the assembly programs, and how to build the basic components of processors using digital logic. Topics include assembly programming, combinational and sequential logic, processor performance, processor design, and the memory hierarchy.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 15L or CSE 29 or ECE 15; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: First-year Student Seminar
courses.description: The First-year Student Seminar Program is designed to provide new students with the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member in a small seminar setting. First-year student seminars are offered in all campus departments and undergraduate colleges, and topics vary from quarter to quarter. Enrollment is limited to fifteen to twenty students, with preference given to entering first-year students.
courses.prerequisites_text: none.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Science and Engineering Seminar
courses.description: A seminar format discussion led by CSE faculty on topics in central areas of computer science, concentrating on the relation among them, recent developments, and future directions. This seminar introduces incoming students to resources and opportunities in the CSE department. May be taken for credit up to three times. Restricted to students in the CSE-PACE program.
courses.prerequisites_text: none.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Tutor Apprenticeship
courses.description: Students assigned to tutor for a CSE course for the first time receive individual and group mentoring and training on how to be effective tutors to help them develop the skills and tools needed to be effective in their tutor role. Students must have a concurrent tutor appointment in a CSE course. See CSE website for application information.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Advanced Data Structures
courses.description: High-performance data structures and supporting algorithms. Use and implementation of data structures like (un)balanced trees, graphs, priority queues, and hash tables. Also, memory management, pointers, recursion. Theoretical and practical performance analysis, both average case and amortized. Uses C++ and STL. Recommended preparation: background in C or C++ programming.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 21 or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 and CSE 12 and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or ECE 15; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits. Students may not receive credit for both CSE 100R and CSE 100.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Advanced Data Structures
courses.description: High-performance data structures and supporting algorithms. Use and implementation of data structures like (un)balanced trees, graphs, priority queues, and hash tables. Also memory management, pointers, recursion. Theoretical and practical performance analysis, both average case and amortized. Uses C++ and STL.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 21 or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 and CSE 12 and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or ECE 15. This course is a distance education course. Students may not receive credit for both CSE 100R and CSE 100.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
courses.description: Design and analysis of efficient algorithms with emphasis of nonnumerical algorithms such as sorting, searching, pattern matching, and graph and network algorithms. Measuring complexity of algorithms, time and storage. NP-complete problems.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 21 or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 and CSE 12 or DSC 30; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: A Practical Introduction to Probability and Statistics
courses.description: Distributions over the real line. Independence, expectation, conditional expectation, mean, variance. Hypothesis testing. Learning classifiers. Distributions over R^n, covariance matrix. Binomial, Poisson distributions. Chernoff bound. Entropy. Compression. Arithmetic coding. Maximal likelihood estimation. Bayesian estimation. CSE 103 is not duplicate credit for ECE 109, ECON 120A, or MATH 183.
courses.prerequisites_text: MATH 20B and CSE 21 or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS28, and CS29 majors. Other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Theory of Computability
courses.description: An introduction to the mathematical theory of computability. Formal languages. Finite automata and regular expressions. Push-down automata and context-free languages. Computable or recursive functions: Turing machines, the halting problem. Undecidability.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 and CSE 20 or MATH 109 or MATH 15A or MATH 31CH and CSE 21 or MATH 100A or MATH 103A or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, EC26, and MA30 majors. Other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Modern Cryptography
courses.description: Topics include private and public-key cryptography, block ciphers, data encryption, authentication, key distribution and certification, pseudorandom number generators, design and analysis of protocols, zero-knowledge proofs, and advanced protocols. Emphasizes rigorous mathematical approach including formal definitions of security goals and proofs of protocol security.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 21 or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 and CSE 101 and CSE 105; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS28, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Software Engineering
courses.description: Introduction to software development and engineering methods, including specification, design, implementation, testing, and process. An emphasis on team development, agile methods, and use of tools such as IDE’s, version control, and test harnesses.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 100 or CSE 100R; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Ubiquitous Computing
courses.description: Explores emerging opportunities enabled by cheap sensors and networked computing devices. Small research projects will be conducted in teams, culminating in project presentations at the end of the term. Section will cover material relevant to the project, such as research methods, software engineering, teamwork, and project management.
courses.prerequisites_text: any course from the following: COGS 102C or COGS 121 or COGS 184 or COGS 184GS or CSE 131 or CSE 132B or ECE 111 or ECE 118 or ECE 191 or ECE 192.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Operating Systems Principles
courses.description: Introduces operating systems concepts, including processes, synchronization, scheduling, memory management, virtual memory, file systems, and protection. May be coscheduled with CSE 220.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 15L or CSE 29 and CSE 30 and CSE 100 or CSE 100R and CSE 101; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Security
courses.description: Topics include basic cryptography, security/threat analysis, access control, auditing, security models, distributed systems security, and theory behind common attack and defense techniques. The class will go over formal models as well as the bits and bytes of security exploits.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 21 or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 and CSE 120 or CSE 123 or CSE 124 or ECE 158A or ECE 158B; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS28, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Programming Languages: Principles and Paradigms
courses.description: (Formerly CSE 173.) Introduction to programming languages and paradigms, the components that comprise them, and the principles of language design, all through the analysis and comparison of a variety of languages (e.g., Pascal, Ada, C++, PROLOG, ML.) Will involve programming in most languages studied.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 and CSE 100 or CSE 100R and CSE 105; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Compiler Construction
courses.description: (Formerly CSE 131B.) Introduction to the compilation of programming languages, practice of syntax-directed translation, type checking, code generation, optimization, interpretation, and compiler structure. Students may receive repeat credit for CSE 131A and CSE 131B by completing CSE 131. May be coscheduled with CSE 231.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 30 and CSE 100 or CSE 100R and CSE 105 and CSE 130; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Database System Principles
courses.description: Basic concepts of databases, including data modeling, relational databases, query languages, optimization, dependencies, schema design, and concurrency control. Exposure to one or several commercial database systems. Advanced topics such as deductive and object-oriented databases, time allowing.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 100 or CSE 100R; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, EC26, CS27, CS28, and CS29 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Web Client Languages
courses.description: Design and implementation of interactive World Wide Web clients using helper applications and plug-ins. The main language covered will be Java.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 100 or CSE 100R; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Components and Design Techniques for Digital Systems
courses.description: Design of Boolean logic and finite state machines; two-level, multilevel combinational logic design, combinational modules and modular networks, Mealy and Moore machines, analysis and synthesis of canonical forms, sequential modules.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 30 or ECE 30; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Digital Systems Laboratory
courses.description: Implementation with computer-aided design tools for combinational logic minimization and state machine synthesis. Hardware construction of a small digital system.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 30; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Architecture
courses.description: Introduction to computer architecture. Computer system design. Processor design. Control design. Memory systems. Two units of credit offered for CSE 141 if CSE 142 taken previously.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 30 or ECE 30 and CSE 140; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Project in Computer Architecture
courses.description: Hands-on computer architecture project aiming to familiarize students with instruction set architecture, and design of process. Control and memory systems.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 30 or ECE 30 and CSE 140; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS28, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Architecture: A Software Perspective
courses.description: This course covers the operation, structure, and programming interfaces of modern CPUs with an emphasis on exploiting processor features to improve software performance and efficiency. The topics covered in this course include performance, energy, x86 assembly, compiler optimizations, pipelining, instruction-level parallelism, caches, memory-level parallelism, multi-threading, multi-core processors, and SIMD. Two units of credit offered for CSE 142 if CSE 141 taken previously or concurrently.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 30 or ECE 30 and CSE 100 or CSE 100R. Restricted to students within CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence: Probabilistic Reasoning and Decision-Making
courses.description: Introduction to probabilistic models at the heart of modern artificial intelligence. Specific topics to be covered include probabilistic methods for reasoning and decision-making under uncertainty; inference and learning in Bayesian networks; prediction and planning in Markov decision processes; applications to intelligent systems, speech and natural language processing, information retrieval, and robotics.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 or DSC 40B and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80 and COGS 118D or CSE 103 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 or MATH 180A or MATH 180B or MATH 181A or MATH 183 or MATH 186 and MATH 20A and MATH 18 or MATH 31AH; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, EC26, and DS25 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence: Search and Reasoning
courses.description: The course will introduce important ideas and algorithms in search and reasoning and demonstrate how they are used in practical AI applications. Topics include A* search, adversarial search, Monte Carlo tree search, reinforcement learning, constraint solving and optimization, propositional and first-order reasoning.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 or DSC 40B and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80 and COGS 118D or CSE 103 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 or MATH 180A or MATH 180B or MATH 181A or MATH 183 or MATH 186 and CSE 100 or CSE 100R; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, EC26, and DS25 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Machine Learning: Learning Algorithms
courses.description: Broad introduction to machine learning. The topics include some topics in supervised learning, such as k-nearest neighbor classifiers, decision trees, boosting, and perceptrons; and topics in unsupervised learning, such as k-means and hierarchical clustering. In addition to the actual algorithms, the course focuses on the principles behind the algorithms. Students may not receive credit for both CSE 151A and COGS 188. May be coscheduled with CSE 251A.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 or DSC 40B and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80 and COGS 118D or CSE 103 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 or MATH 180A or MATH 180B or MATH 181A or MATH 183 or MATH 186 and MATH 18 or MATH 31AH and MATH 20C or MATH 31BH; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, EC26, and DS25 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Vision I
courses.description: This course provides a broad introduction to the foundations, algorithms, and applications of computer vision. It introduces classical models and contemporary methods, from image formation models to deep learning, to address problems of 3-D reconstruction and object recognition from images and video. Topics include filtering, feature detection, stereo vision, structure from motion, motion estimation, and recognition. Programming assignments will be in Python. Students may not receive credit for both CSE 152A and CSE 152.
courses.prerequisites_text: MATH 18 or MATH 31AH and CSE 12 or DSC 30 and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80; Python programming experience recommended; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Recommender Systems and Web Mining
courses.description: Current methods for data mining and predictive analytics. Emphasis is on studying real-world data sets, building working systems, and putting current ideas from machine learning research into practice.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 or DSC 40B and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80 and BENG 100 or BENG 134 or COGS 118D or CSE 103 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 or MATH 180A or MATH 180B or MATH 181A or MATH 183 or MATH 186; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, EC26, and DS25 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits. May be coscheduled with CSE 258. Students may not receive credit for CSE 158 and CSE 158R or DSC 148.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Recommender Systems and Web Mining
courses.description: Current methods for data mining and predictive analytics. Emphasis is on studying real-world data sets, building working systems, and putting current ideas from machine learning research into practice.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 or DSC 40B and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80 and BENG 100 or BENG 134 or COGS 118D or CSE 103 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 or MATH 180A or MATH 180B or MATH 181A or MATH 183 or MATH 186; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS28, CS29, EC26, and DS25 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits. This course is a distance education course. May be coscheduled with CSE 258R. Students may not receive credit for CSE 158R and CSE 158 or DSC 148.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Computer Graphics
courses.description: Representation and manipulation of pictorial data. Two-dimensional and three-dimensional transformations, curves, surfaces. Projection, illumination, and shading models. Raster and vector graphic I/O devices; retained-mode and immediate-mode graphics software systems and applications. Students may not receive credit for CSE 167 and CSE 167R or MATH 155A.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 100 or CSE 100R; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Interaction Design
courses.description: Introduces fundamental methods and principles for designing, implementing, and evaluating user interfaces. Topics include user-centered design, rapid prototyping, experimentation, direct manipulation, cognitive principles, visual design, social software, software tools. Learn by doing: Work with a team on a quarter-long design project. Students may not receive credit for COGS 120 and CSE 170. Recommended preparation: Basic familiarity with HTML.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 108 or CSE 12 or DSC 30 and COGS 1 or COGS 10 or DSGN 1 or ENG 100D.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics in Computer Science and Engineering
courses.description: Topics of special interest in computer science and engineering. Topics may vary from quarter to quarter. May be repeated for credit with the consent of instructor. May be taken for credit up to three times. May be coscheduled with CSE 291.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Seminar in CSE
courses.description: A seminar course on topics of current interest. Students, as well as the instructor, will be actively involved in running the course/class. This course cannot be counted toward a technical elective.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Science Research
courses.description: Introduction to research in computer science. Topics include defining a CS research problem, finding and reading technical papers, oral communication, technical writing, and independent learning. Course participants apprentice with a CSE research group and propose an original research project.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of the department chair. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Race, Gender, and Computing
courses.description: This course explores the challenges of diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) in computing and technology through an introduction to and analysis of various social constructs and their impact on not only computing-related organizations, but also the technologies developed and the people affected by them. This course also introduces students to cultural competence in the context of computing.
courses.prerequisites_text: AAS 10 or CSE 12 or ECE 35 or ETHN 3 or HILD 7A or LTEN 27 and CAT 125 or CAT 125R or CAT 3 or DOC 3 or HUM 2 or MCWP 125 or MCWP 125R or MCWP 50 or MCWP 50R or MMW 121 or MMW 121R or MMW 122 or MMW 13 or SYN 2 or WCWP 100 or WCWP 10B.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Field Study in Computer Science and Engineering
courses.description: Directed study accompanying full-time on-site computer science internships. (P/NP grades only.)
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of the instructor and approval of the department required. Students may receive credit for one of the following: CSE 197 or CSE 197C. Restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, and CS29 majors only.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Directed Group Study
courses.description: Computer science and engineering topics whose study involves reading and discussion by a small group of students under the supervision of a faculty member. (P/NP grades only.)
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of the instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Independent Study for Undergraduates
courses.description: Independent reading or research by special arrangement with a faculty member. (P/NP grades only.)
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of the instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: CSE Honors Thesis Research for Undergraduates
courses.description: Undergraduate research for completing an honors project under the supervision of a CSE faculty member. May be taken across multiple quarters. Students should enroll for a letter grade. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: Admission to the CSE department honors program. Consent of the instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Algorithm Design and Analysis
courses.description: The basic techniques for the design and analysis of algorithms. Divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, data structures, graph search, algebraic problems, randomized algorithms, lower bounds, probabilistic analysis, parallel algorithms. Recommended preparation: Understanding of design and analysis of efficient algorithms with emphasis of nonnumerical algorithms such as sorting, searching, pattern matching, and graph and network algorithms. Restricted to students within the CS75, CS78, CS89, CS88, CS77, CS80, CS81, CS83, and CS76 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Lattice Algorithms and Applications
courses.description: (Formerly CSE 207C) Introduction to the algorithmic theory of point lattices (aka algorithmic geometry of numbers), and some of its most important applications in cryptography and cryptanalysis. Topics usually include LLL basis reduction algorithm, cryptanalysis of broadcast RSA, hardness of approximating lattice problems.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 202, CSE 200, or concurrent.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics/Seminar in Algorithms, Complexity, and Logic
courses.description: Topics of special interest in algorithms, complexity, and logic to be presented by faculty and students under faculty direction. Topics vary from quarter to quarter. May be repeated for credit.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics/Seminar in Cryptography
courses.description: Topics of special interest in cryptography to be presented by faculty and students under faculty direction. Topics vary from quarter to quarter. May be repeated for credit.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Principles of Software Engineering
courses.description: (Formerly CSE 264A.) General principles in modern software engineering. Both theoretical and practical topics are covered. Theoretical topics include proofs of correctness, programming language semantics, and theory of testing. Practical topics include structured programming, modularization techniques, design of languages for reliable programming, and software tools. Restricted to students within the CS75, CS78, CS89, CS88, CS77, CS80, CS81, CS83, and CS76 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Research Topics in Human-Computer Interaction
courses.description: Prepares students to conduct original HCI research by reading and discussing seminal and cutting-edge research papers. Topics include design, social software, input techniques, mobile, and ubiquitous computing. Student pairs perform a quarter-long mini research project that leverages campus research efforts. Cross-listed with COGS 230.
courses.prerequisites_text: none.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Design at Large
courses.description: New societal challenges, cultural values, and technological opportunities are changing design—and vice versa. The seminar explores this increased scale, real-world engagement, and disruptive impact. Invited speakers from UC San Diego and beyond share cutting-edge research on interaction, design, and learning. Cross-listed with COGS 229. (S/U grades only.)
courses.prerequisites_text: none.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Operating Systems
courses.description: Operating system structures, concurrent computation models, scheduling, synchronization mechanisms, address spaces, memory management protection and security, buffering, streams, data-copying reduction techniques, file systems, naming, caching, disk organization, mapped files, remote file systems, case studies of major operating systems.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 120 and 121, or consent of instructor. Restricted to students within the CS75, CS78, CS89, CS88, CS77, CS80, CS81, CS83, and CS76 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Computer Security
courses.description: Security and threat models, risk analysis, authentication and authorization, auditing, operating systems security, access control mechanisms, protection mechanisms, distributed systems/network security, security architecture, electronic commerce security mechanisms, security evaluation.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 221 or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics/Seminar in Computer Systems
courses.description: Discussion on problems of current research interest in computer systems. Possible areas of focus include distributed computing, computational grid, operating systems, fault-tolerant computing, storage systems, system services for the World Wide Web. Topics to be presented by faculty and students under faculty direction. Topics vary from quarter to quarter. May be repeated for credit.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics/Seminar in Computer Security
courses.description: Discussion on problems of current research interest in computer security. Topics to be presented by faculty and students under faculty direction. Topics vary from quarter to quarter. May be repeated for credit.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Validation and Testing of Embedded Systems
courses.description: Embedded system building blocks including IP cores. Cosimulation. Formal verification using model checking. Verification environments. Test challenges in core integration: compliance, feature, random, and collision testing. Core access and test integration. Interface-based verification and standards.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 237A; or basic courses in algorithms and data structures, elementary calculus, discrete math, symbolic logic, computer architecture; or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics/Seminar in Programming Languages
courses.description: Discussion on problems of current research interest in programming languages, formal methods, and software engineering. Possible areas of focus include program verification, program synthesis, language design and implementation, developer productivity tools, language-based security. Topics to be presented by faculty and students under faculty direction. Topics vary from quarter to quarter. May be taken for credit up to eighteen times for a maximum of eighteen units.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Principles of Computer Architecture
courses.description: (Formerly CSE 240.) This course will cover fundamental concepts in computer architecture. Topics include instruction set architecture, pipelining, pipeline hazards, bypassing, dynamic scheduling, branch prediction, superscalar issue, memory-hierarchy design, advanced cache architectures, and multiprocessor architecture issues. Restricted to students within the CS75, CS78, CS89, CS88, CS77, CS80, CS81, CS83, and CS76 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Seminar in Embedded Systems
courses.description: Topics of special interest to researchers in embedded systems and mobile computing to be presented by faculty and students under faculty direction. Topics vary from quarter to quarter. Representative work usually found at venues such as CPS-IOT Week, SenSys, MobiCom, MobiSys, ESWEEK, and IMWUT (UbiComp). May be taken up to twenty-four times for credit.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Principles of Artificial Intelligence: Probabilistic Reasoning and Learning
courses.description: Methods based on probability theory for reasoning and learning under uncertainty. Content may include directed and undirected probabilistic graphical models, exact and approximate inference, latent variables, expectation-maximization, hidden Markov models, Markov decision processes, applications to vision, robotics, speech, and/or text. Recommended preparation: CSE 103 or similar course.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing. Restricted to students within the CS75, CS78, CS89, CS88, CS77, CS80, CS81, CS83, and CS76 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits. Recommended preparation: understanding of probability and statistics.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Computer Vision I
courses.description: Comprehensive introduction to computer vision providing broad coverage including low-level vision (image formation, photometry, color, image feature detection), inferring 3-D properties from images (shape-from shading, stereo vision, motion interpretation) and object recognition. Companion to CSE 252B covering complementary topics. Restricted to students within the CS75, CS78, CS89, CS88, CS77, CS80, CS81, CS83, and CS76 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Recommender Systems and Web Mining
courses.description: Current methods for data mining and predictive analytics. Emphasis is on studying real-world data sets, building working systems, and putting current ideas from machine learning research into practice. Recommended preparation: No previous background in machine learning is required, but students should be comfortable with programming (all example code will be in Python), and with basic optimization and linear algebra. Recommended preparation: No previous background in machine learning is required, but students should be comfortable with programming (all example code will be in Python). Restricted to students within the CS75, CS78, CS89, CS88, CS77, CS80, CS81, CS83, and CS76 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits. May be coscheduled with CSE 158. Students will not receive credit for both CSE 258 and CSE 258R.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Recommender Systems and Web Mining
courses.description: Current methods for data mining and predictive analytics. Emphasis is on studying real-world data sets, building working systems, and putting current ideas from machine learning research into practice. Recommended preparation: No previous background in machine learning is required, but students should be comfortable with programming (all example code will be in Python), and with basic optimization and linear algebra. This will be a fully online class based on extensive educational materials and an online educational platform. May be coscheduled with CSE 158R. Students may not receive credit for CSE 258R and CSE 258.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Seminar in Artificial Intelligence
courses.description: A weekly meeting featuring local (and occasional external) speakers discussing their current research in artificial intelligence neural networks, and genetic algorithms. (S/U grades only.)
courses.prerequisites_text: none.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Parallel Computation
courses.description: (Formerly CSE 274A.) This course provides an overview of parallel hardware, algorithms, models, and software. Topics include Flynn’s taxonomy, interconnection networks, memory organization, a survey of commercially available multiprocessors, parallel algorithm paradigms and complexity criteria, parallel programming environments and tools for parallel debugging, language specification, mapping, performance, etc. Restricted to students within the CS75, CS78, CS89, CS88, CS77, CS80, CS81, CS83, and CS76 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Discrete Differential Geometry
courses.description: This course introduces the mathematics and algorithms for digital geometry processing and simulation problems in computer graphics. Topics include the continuous and discrete theory of curves and surfaces, exterior calculus, Hodge theory, and gauge theory with various applications ranging from texture synthesis, differential equations, and vector field design. Restricted to CS75, CS76, CS78, CS88, and CS89 majors. Other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Robotics
courses.description: This course provides an introduction to the fundamentals of robotics across kinematics, sensor systems, estimation, control, and planning. The contents include introduction to robotics in general, kinematics of robot systems, robot arm systems, sensors for robots, basic vision for robots, estimation methods, perception, robot localization and navigation, control of robot systems, robot motion planning, robot task planning, robot architectures, and evaluation of robot systems. It is expected that students have a solid understanding of linear algebra, can program in Python or C++, and have a basic understanding of methods for reasoning under uncertainty.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing. Restricted to students within the CS75, CS78, CS89, CS88, CS77, CS80, CS81, CS83, and CS76 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Seminar in Computer Science and Engineering
courses.description: (Formerly CSE 280A.) A seminar course in which topics of special interest in computer science and engineering will be presented by staff members and graduate students under faculty direction. Topics vary from quarter to quarter. May be repeated for credit. (S/U grades only.)
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor. (Offered as faculty resources permit.)

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics in Artificial Intelligence
courses.description: Topics of special interest in artificial intelligence in computer science and engineering. Topics may vary quarter to quarter. May be taken for credit up to ten times.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics in Programming Languages, Compilers, and Software Engineering
courses.description: Topics of special interest in programming languages, compilers, and software engineering in computer science and engineering. Topics may vary quarter to quarter. May be taken for credit up to ten times.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics in Theoretical Computer Science
courses.description: Topics of special interest in theoretical computer science in computer science and engineering. Topics may vary quarter to quarter. May be taken for credit up to ten times.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics in Computer Systems and Security
courses.description: Topics of special interest in systems and security in computer science and engineering. Topics may vary quarter to quarter. May be taken for credit up to ten times.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Faculty Research Seminar
courses.description: (Formerly CSE 282.) Computer science and engineering faculty will present one-hour seminars of the current research work in their areas of interest.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE graduate status.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Special Project in Computer Science and Engineering
courses.description: The student will conceive, design, and execute a project in computer science under the direction of a faculty member. The project will typically include a large programming or hardware design task, but other types of projects are possible.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE graduate student status. (CS 75, 76, 77, 78, 79, 80, 81) (S/U grades only.)

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Research Meeting in CSE
courses.description: Advanced study and analysis of active research in computer science and computer engineering. Discussion of current research and literature in the research specialty of the staff member teaching the course.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.description: Open to properly qualified graduate students who wish to pursue a problem through advanced study under the direction of a member of the staff. (S/U grades only.)
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Research
courses.description: Research.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of faculty.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Teaching Assistantship
courses.description: A course in which teaching assistants are aided in learning proper teaching methods by means of supervision of their work by the faculty: handling of discussions, preparation and grading of examinations and other written exercises, and student relations. May be used to meet teaching experience requirement for candidates for the PhD degree. Number of units for credit depends on number of hours devoted to class or section assistance.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing and consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Teaching Methods in Computer Science
courses.description: Training in teaching methods in the field of computer science. This course examines theoretical and practical communication and teaching techniques particularly appropriate to computer science.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of faculty.

courses.subject: CCE
courses.title: Critical Approaches in Community Practice
courses.description: Introduces ethical partnership across complex social, historical, and political positions. The course addresses contested framings of community and participation through practical examples, theoretical conceptions, and empirical studies. Students will give close attention to shared circumstance and negotiation of power relations. Must be taken for a letter grade to count toward Eighth College general-education requirements.
courses.prerequisites_text: Eighth College students only; completion of UC Entry Level Writing Requirement.

courses.subject: CCE
courses.title: Cultivating Community-Informed Practices
courses.description: This course introduces students to writing as a community-informed endeavor. Students will develop writing practices to engage in respectful, meaningful, ethical, and reciprocal community partnerships. Using participatory action and community-rooted research, students will develop reading, writing, and thinking practices that recognize, honor, and foster community knowledge. Must be taken for a letter grade to count toward Eighth College general-education requirements.
courses.prerequisites_text: Eighth College students only; CCE 1.

courses.subject: CCE
courses.title: Elements of Community-Engaged Collaborative Research
courses.description: This course introduces students to community-engaged collaborative research and community-facing writing. Students develop practices for negotiation, ongoing reflection and revision, and methods for recognizing who is not present and why. This course prepares students to build processes for navigating opportunities and challenges, using research and writing as a foundation for engagement, critical thinking, creative practice, communication, and revision.
courses.prerequisites_text: Eighth College students only; CCE 2.

courses.subject: CGS
courses.title: Introduction to Critical Gender Studies: Key Terms and Concepts
courses.description: This course will be a general introduction to the key terms, issues, and concepts in the fields of gender and sexuality studies.

courses.subject: CGS
courses.title: Conceptualizing Gender: Theoretical Approaches
courses.description: This course explores the significance of gender as a category of analysis by examining diverse theoretical frameworks from the field of critical gender studies. Particular attention is given to gender in relation to race, class, sexuality, nation, (dis)ability, and religion. Students will not receive credit for both CGS 100 and 100A.
courses.prerequisites_text: CGS 2A-B or at least one CGS upper-division course.

courses.subject: CGS
courses.title: Sexual Violence
courses.description: This course examines how sexual violence is experienced in relation to/with gender, racialization, sexuality, and class. It considers reporting structures and asks who is heard when sexual violence is named and how so many are not heard. It also explores movements working to interrupt sexual violence.
